payload.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=metrics+for+novelty+and+feasibility+in+autonomous+research+candidate+selection&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Unifying AI-assisted scientific discovery around exploration, hypothesis generation, and testing\", \"abstract\": null, \"doi\": null, \"pmid\": \"PMC13674306\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13674306\", \"source\": \"PMC\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13674306/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"PubMedCentral\", \"url\": \"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13674306/pdf/?tool=EBI\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13674306\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13674306?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"AI-Driven Synthesis in Medicinal Chemistry: Integrating Large Language Models, Robotic Automation, and Sustainability Metrics to Accelerate Drug Discovery.\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming synthetic chemistry from task-specific predictors into integrated platforms that unify retrosynthesis, reaction optimization, and closed-loop robotic automation. This review highlights how AI-assisted planning and robotic execution shorten cycle times, reduce step counts, and improve route sustainability in medicinal chemistry. Recent advances, including large language models (LLMs), template-free retrosynthesis, and Bayesian optimization, are evaluated alongside key limitations in dataset quality, reproducibility, and deployment costs. To ensure translational relevance, reproducible benchmarks such as step count, time-to-in vitro, and green metrics (E-factor, process mass intensity) are emphasized. This review proposes a hierarchical framework structured across three interconnected levels: cognitive planning, physical execution, and translational evaluation. Within this structure, key elements include LLM-based synthesis planning, robotic and closed-loop execution, interpretable decision-making, sustainability-by-design, advanced reaction optimization, and multi-objective retrosynthesis. Together, these components provide a conceptual basis for integrating digital intelligence with physical experimentation. By embedding green chemistry principles and regulatory awareness, AI is increasingly positioned not only as a predictive tool but also as an assistive collaborator supporting decision-making in medicinal chemistry workflows. The convergence of AI, robotics, and sustainability metrics highlights an emerging transition; however, realizing a future where every experiment reliably feeds back into autonomous learning loops requires overcoming significant current barriers in data standardization and hardware interoperability.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/med.70074\", \"pmid\": \"42310963\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13637048\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/med.70074\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13637048\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13637048?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"ST-GICM: A Spatiotemporal Graph Learning Framework with Intrinsic Curiosity for Robust Autonomous Exploration.\", \"abstract\": \"With recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) and graph neural networks (GNNs), graph-based autonomous exploration methods have significantly improved decision-making performance in complex environments. However, under partial observability and sparse-reward conditions, existing methods still struggle with long-horizon decision-making and sustained exploration. To address these challenges, we propose a spatiotemporal graph learning framework, termed ST-GICM, that improves the robustness and efficiency of autonomous exploration by integrating graph-structured encoding, temporal memory, and an intrinsic curiosity mechanism. Specifically, a Graph Attention Network (GAT) and a Spatiotemporal Reasoning Core (STRC) are employed to dynamically encode the viewpoint graph and fuse temporal memory, thereby alleviating perceptual aliasing in graph-based exploration. In addition, an Intrinsic Prediction Module (IPM) is designed to generate intrinsic rewards based on the prediction error of graph-level latent representations, thereby encouraging sustained exploration. Experiments conducted in procedurally generated complex topological environments show that the proposed method outperforms existing baselines in terms of coverage rate, success rate, repeated revisit rate, and oscillation count, while maintaining trajectory costs comparable to those of the baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of ST-GICM in partially observable environments under sparse-reward conditions.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/s26113307\", \"pmid\": \"42280827\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13259222\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/s26113307\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13259222\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13259222?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Beyond Permeability Prediction: Machine Learning for Gas-Separation Membranes from Data Curation to Experimentally Validated Discovery.\", \"abstract\": \"Machine learning (ML) is transforming gas-separation membrane research, yet high retrospective accuracy does not necessarily translate into experimentally viable or process-relevant materials. This review reframes the field around the evidence chain required to convert a membrane record into a defensible discovery decision. Across polymers, metal-organic and covalent organic frameworks, mixed-matrix membranes, carbon molecular sieves, and two-dimensional systems, we critically examine data curation, physics-aligned representation, multitask and multi-fidelity learning, uncertainty quantification, inverse design, and prospective validation. We introduce a five-level evidence framework spanning retrospective interpolation, domain-disjoint generalization, physics or simulation confirmation, prospective membrane validation, and deployment-relevant testing. We further propose a contextualized observation unit that binds chemical identity to membrane state, fabrication history, feed composition, operating conditions, time, protocol, and provenance, thereby exposing leakage and structural uncertainty hidden by conventional datasets. Our analysis shows that ML has demonstrably accelerated data completion, simulation, and candidate prioritization, whereas evidence for routinely discovering manufacturable, durable, mixed-gas-performing membranes remains limited and concentrated in polymer studies. To close this gap, we develop a constrained, uncertainty-aware closed-loop architecture that treats feasibility and fabrication failures as learnable outcomes, couples acquisition to multiscale process utility, and advances candidates through staged experimental fidelities. A minimum reporting standard and measurable research priorities are provided. Together, these contributions propose \\\"decision-grade ML\\\" as an emerging framework for evaluating machine learning in membrane science: models should know their applicability domain, preserve physical context, propose feasible experiments, quantify uncertainty under domain shift, and demonstrate value under the conditions of intended membrane use rather than merely reproduce familiar labels or idealized proxies.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/membranes16100340\", \"pmid\": \"42931018\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13707221\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\":
